title: How "OK" was born
hook: A word now heard all over the world began as a newspaper joke in 1839 Boston.
peek: "OK" began as a joke abbreviation for "oll korrect" in a Boston newspaper in 1839. A presidential campaign the next year spread it across America, and from there it reached nearly every language on Earth.
lede: In the late 1830s, Boston newspapers had a fad for jokey abbreviations of deliberately misspelled phrases. On 23 March 1839 the Boston Morning Post printed "o.k.", standing for "oll korrect". Most of these jokes vanished within months. This one survived, and today it is often described as one of the most widely used words in the world.

bullets.text: For a long time nobody knew where OK came from. In the 1960s the American scholar Allen Walker Read traced it through old newspapers to the Boston article, an account most linguists now accept.
In the 1840 election, supporters of President Martin Van Buren, nicknamed Old Kinderhook after his hometown, formed O.K. Clubs. The pun gave the word a second meaning and a national stage.
Old Kinderhook joined a long line of everyday words built from a name. The sandwich took its name from an 18th-century earl who wanted food he could eat at his desk.
Rival stories trace OK to the Choctaw word "okeh", to West African languages or to Scottish "och aye". None has the written evidence behind it, and the documentary trail points to the Boston joke.
Its two quick letters suited telegraph operators, who used it to confirm that a message had arrived. That practical, everyday role helped OK move from passing slang into ordinary speech and writing.
OK is a real word with a silly beginning. Dictionaries also have a few words that began as mistakes, including one that slipped into Webster's in 1934 and never meant anything at all.
